reason: The sources provide 15 detailed, multi-site-verified claims about the physics, history, and future of the Big Dipper.
story: The Big Dipper is an astronomical illusion. While it looks like a permanent fixture of the northern sky, its stars are not all physically bound together. In 1869, astronomer Richard Proctor discovered that the 'inner five' stars—Merak, Phecda, Megrez, Alioth, and Mizar—are siblings born from the same nebula about 500 million years ago. They belong to the Ursa Major Moving Group, drifting together toward Sagittarius at 31,000 miles per hour. However, the stars at the ends, Dubhe and Alkaid, are total strangers moving in the opposite direction. Because they aren't all tied together, this cosmic tug-of-war is slowly warping the iconic spoon. In roughly 50,000 to 100,000 years, the handle will bend and the bowl will open up until the 'dipper' vanishes entirely, re-forming into a completely different shape. Even our Sun is currently a temporary guest drifting through the outskirts of this stellar stream.
angle: Five stars of the Big Dipper are 'siblings' traveling together, while the two stars at the ends are total strangers moving in the opposite direction, meaning the famous 'spoon' will eventually break apart.

claims.claim: The Big Dipper is an asterism, not a constellation, and is located within the larger constellation Ursa Major.
The asterism is composed of seven bright stars that form the shape of a ladle or dipper.
In 1869, British astronomer Richard Proctor discovered that many of the Dipper's stars share a common proper motion through space.
Five of the stars—Merak, Phecda, Megrez, Alioth, and Mizar—belong to a physical group called the Ursa Major Moving Group.
These five member stars share a common origin and are estimated to be between 400 and 500 million years old.
The core of the Ursa Major Moving Group is located approximately 75 to 80 light-years away from Earth.
The stars Dubhe and Alkaid, which sit at the ends of the asterism, are not part of the moving group.
Dubhe and Alkaid are moving in the opposite direction relative to the other five stars.
The differing velocities of the seven stars will eventually cause the Big Dipper's shape to dissolve.
Astronomers predict the asterism will re-form into a new shape in approximately 50,000 to 100,000 years.
The Ursa Major Moving Group is currently traveling toward a point in the constellation Sagittarius.
The solar system is currently drifting through the outskirts of this stellar stream but is not a physical member of the group.
The stars Merak and Dubhe are known as the Pointers because a line through them leads directly to the North Star, Polaris.
Observing the star Alcor next to Mizar in the Dipper's handle has traditionally been used as a test of visual acuity.
The Ursa Major Moving Group was once a tightly bound open cluster that has since dispersed over a region 30 light-years long.

disputed: The exact age of the group is cited as 400 million years in some sources and 500 million in others; the script should use a range.
The timeframe for the shape change varies between 50,000 and 100,000 years; the script should attribute this as an approximation.
The membership of Sirius in the group is disputed, with newer research suggesting it is a coincidental neighbor; the script should omit Sirius to remain accurate.
